The narrator's windows look across the roofs of a crowded city.
The life seen at neighbors' windows and on the roofs often suggests the narrator's thoughts.
A little boy lives across the way, one story below the narrator's home, with his parents.
The boy has been ill for several weeks.
The boy stays in bed after the rest of his household is up and dressed, with books and toys piled around him.
The boy sometimes raises his knees under the covers to make a snowy mountain and leads paper soldiers up its slope.
The boy's kitten sometimes romps on the bedcover and pounces on his toes, and at other times sleeps on the sunny windowsill.
Judging by the boy's rapt attention, his book is about far-off islands and coconut trees.
The boy is brought a yellow drink of eggs and milk in the afternoon.
The eggnog drink is a favorite of the boy's, judging by how eagerly he licks his lips.
The boy has recently been pressing his nose eagerly against the window, which shows he is recovering.
As the days grow short and lights are needed, domestic scenes appear as shadows on the curtains of another set of windows.
Hurry and changing of clothes behind the curtains suggest that the neighbors are getting ready for a party.
Once their upstairs lights go out, the neighbors will come out of their door below in shiny evening clothes.
The narrator wishes the neighbors a pleasant dinner, with ice cream for dessert.
The narrator has a sweet tooth.
A kitchen window is also opposite, where savory dishes can be seen cooking on the fire.
The cook stirs the food with an unusually long iron spoon.
The old saying holds that whoever sups with the devil needs a long spoon.
The kitchen spoon is long enough that someone dining with the devil could safely eat from the shared pot.
The proverb about supping with the devil surely does not apply to the quiet street.
Many stories lower there is a section of roof furnished with wicker furniture and a row of bright plants along the gutter.
Every afternoon at exactly six, when that roof is in shadow, a man comes out there and reads his evening paper.
The man's wife later joins him, and they eat supper from a tray.
The couple sits nearly at the bottom of a well of buildings that cuts them off from the world, like the hedge of a fairy garden.
The couple stays seated on the roof after the tray has been taken away.
Twilight comes early at the couple's low level.
Like cottagers in a valley, the couple watches daylight still lighting the peaks above them.
Another outdoor roof room sits on a taller building above the narrator.
From below, the bright canvas awning of that higher roof room and the side of its supporting trellis can be seen.
On cool summer evenings, people probably sip coffee in that upper roof room and watch the city's lights come on.
Glimpses of neighbors appear all around: a figure against curtains, a group by the fire in season, the week's darning on a rocking chair, a nose at an open window in the morning.
The roofs themselves make up the main view.
The nearby roofs have gravel surfaces with spouts, spinning vents, and chimneys.
The nearby roofs have posts and clotheslines for washing.
Once a week a laundress pokes her head up through a roof scuttle.
The laundress arrives at almost exactly the same minute each time.
When the scuttle moves, it looks mysterious, as if one of the forty thieves were pushing at the rocks that guard his cave.
The laundress's plain, bouncing figure ends the romantic fancy as soon as her shoulders appear above the scuttle.
The laundress is a good-natured person.
When the wind is right, the laundress can be heard singing as she works.
The laundress tries out popular tunes while her mouth is full of clothespins.
A clothespin once slipped into the laundress's mouth and nearly choked her.
Water tanks stand against the sky on the taller buildings in the distance.
The water tanks are raised on three supports, like fingers holding up a cup.
The water tanks look like the buildings, newly won over to prohibition, raising water cups to pledge the cause with a beginner's excitement.
Hard liquor is stored in a rathskeller below the sidewalk and in kegs in the basement.
The roof has gone dry in triumph over the liquor below.
The row of buildings with water tanks and towers blocks the view to the north.
A crowded world lies beyond those buildings, including the heights of Harlem.
The distant northern scenes cannot be seen from the narrator's windows.
On summer days the roofs bake in the sun, and spirals of heat rise from them.
In the heat, tar oozes from the joints in the tin roofing.
A bright day brings out both tar and the adder.
In the heat, washing hangs limp on the line.
Stockings on the line hang shriveled and lifeless, in contrast to their lively use when worn.
The spouts and chimneys seem to droop in the heavy sunlight.
The spinning vents stop turning in the heat.
August holds its hot midsummer rites on the roofs, as on a steaming altar.
